key_concept: Synergids at the micropylar end of the embryo sac bear a filiform apparatus that guides the pollen tube into the embryo sac for fertilisation.
steps: Recall the typical 7-celled, 8-nucleate (Polygonum-type) embryo sac: an egg apparatus (1 egg + 2 synergids) at the micropylar end, 3 antipodals at the chalazal end, and a central cell with 2 polar nuclei.
Each synergid carries a special cellular thickening at its micropylar tip called the filiform apparatus.
The filiform apparatus secretes chemicals that attract the pollen tube, and the tube enters the embryo sac by penetrating one synergid.
The pollen tube then releases the two male gametes into the cytoplasm of that synergid, from where they move to the egg and the central cell.
Hence the synergids guide the pollen tube for fertilisation.
why_not_others: Antipodals lie at the chalazal end, far from where the pollen tube enters, and are often ephemeral. The central cell and its polar nuclei only take part in triple fusion to form the endosperm; they play no role in guiding the tube.
common_trap: Students often confuse the filiform apparatus (on the synergids) with the egg itself, or think the polar nuclei attract the second male gamete and so guide the tube.
time_saving_tip: Memorise the link 'pollen tube guidance → filiform apparatus → synergids' and mark the answer directly.
